query: W melts near 3422 °C, whereas Cu boils near 2562 °C, so conventional induction or arc-plasma casting cannot readily yield a uniform W–Cu material. Phase separation and void formation can impair thermal transport. Filling a W skeleton with molten Cu or Cu powder can leave defects; spark-plasma sintering and mechanical alloying can produce finer, more uniform structures but can also leave voids; vapor-coated W powders have been sintered to achieve near-perfect contact between the constituents; and metal 3D printing has also been explored. Starting from W particles or connected W regions within a Cu matrix for heat transfer under irradiation in fusion-reactor joints, what single intervention could overcome these limitations while preserving mechanical durability? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention and mechanism, predicts an outcome relative to a named existing fabrication baseline, defines the processing and service boundaries, cites supporting prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment and observations that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Coating W particles with a thin, vapor-deposited Ni interlayer before consolidating them with Cu via spark plasma sintering will promote reactive wetting and graded interfacial bonding that minimizes void formation and phase separation, thereby enhancing both the thermal transport and mechanical durability of the resulting W–Cu composite under fusion-reactor irradiation conditions compared to composites produced by direct vapor coating of W powders.
generation.material_initial_state: W particles or connected W regions embedded in a Cu matrix that, when processed via conventional vapor deposition and sintering methods, exhibit phase separation and voids which impair thermal transport and durability.
generation.intervention: Apply a uniform thin Ni coating on W particles using vapor deposition prior to spark plasma sintering with Cu.
generation.conditions: Processing under spark plasma sintering at temperatures below the boiling point of Cu and within regimes that allow Ni to promote interfacial diffusion; service conditions relevant to high thermal loads and irradiation in fusion-reactor joints.
generation.structural_mediator: A graded interfacial layer formed by the Ni coating that reacts with both W and Cu to improve wetting and reduce interfacial energy, thereby limiting defect formation.
generation.mechanism: The Ni interlayer acts as a reactive wetting agent, reducing the surface energy mismatch and facilitating diffusion bonding between W and Cu. This improved interfacial adhesion minimizes the formation of voids and phase separation during consolidation, leading to enhanced thermal and mechanical performance.
generation.predicted_outcome: The Ni-coated W–Cu composite will exhibit a lower void volume fraction, a more homogenous microstructure, improved thermal conductivity, and better mechanical durability under irradiation compared to the baseline composite fabricated without the Ni interlayer.
generation.baseline: Conventional composites produced by vapor-coating W powders followed by spark plasma sintering, which typically show phase separation, void formation, and compromised thermal transport.
generation.boundary: The intervention is expected to be effective within processing conditions compatible with spark plasma sintering and under fusion-reactor service environments; its effectiveness may diminish if the Ni coating is too thick or if processing temperatures exceed limits that preserve the interfacial structure.
generation.uncertainty: Optimal Ni coating thickness and processing parameters need to be determined, and the long-term irradiation stability of the Ni-mediated interface under fusion-reactor conditions remains to be fully quantified.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of W–Cu composites: one using W particles with a vapor-deposited thin Ni coating and one using uncoated W particles. Consolidate both sets using identical spark plasma sintering parameters. Subject the resulting samples to thermal cycling and simulated irradiation.
measurements: Quantitative porosity and void volume assessment (e.g., via micro-CT imaging)
Mechanical durability tests under simulated irradiation conditions
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Ni-coated composites do not show a statistically significant reduction in void fraction, improved interfacial bonding, higher thermal conductivity, and enhanced mechanical durability under irradiation compared to the uncoated baseline, the hypothesis is falsified.
